title: A common word
hook: come to a word common between us: to worship none but Allah (3:64)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maryam, chosen above the women of the worlds. Your line was chosen and purified. Did you honor a woman of faith out loud? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

In October 2007, a letter went out from Muslim scholars and leaders, more than a hundred and thirty of them, Sunni and Shia, from many countries. It was addressed to the Pope, to Orthodox patriarchs, to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and to the leaders of Christian churches everywhere. Its title was a phrase lifted straight out of a verse in Al 'Imran. The phrase was: a common word between us and you.
screen: `OCTOBER 2007.` → `A LETTER TO CHURCH LEADERS.` → `A PHRASE FROM AL 'IMRAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, 3:64, in Pickthall's words: "Say: O People of the Scripture! Come to an agreement between us and you: that we shall worship none but Allah." Pickthall says agreement. The Arabic is kalimatin sawa', a word that is level, equal, the same for both sides. People of the Scripture, ahl al-kitab, is the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, those given scripture before, in the Qur'an's terms. The verse goes on: that we ascribe no partner to God, and that none of us take others as lords beside God. And if they turn away, it says, then say: bear witness that we are Muslims, those who have surrendered. Notice what the verse doesn't do. It doesn't threaten. It invites, names the ground it believes both sides share, and if the answer is no, it simply asks the other side to witness where Muslims stand. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir connect this part of the surah to a delegation of Christians from Najran who came to Medina to talk with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that when the Prophet wrote to Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor, his letter included this very verse. The 2007 letter took the same phrase and built on two commandments it found in both scriptures: love of God, and love of neighbor. Christian leaders wrote back, and meetings followed. Muslims and Christians still differ on central things, and the verse itself names some of them. But it opens with the word common. It starts the conversation from what is shared.
screen: `KALIMATIN SAWA': A LEVEL WORD` · `AHL AL-KITAB: PEOPLE OF THE SCRIPTURE` · `AN INVITATION, NOT A THREAT` · `FROM HERACLIUS TO 2007` · then, large: `COME TO A COMMON WORD.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, bring to mind a neighbor, a coworker or a relative whose beliefs aren't yours. Picture a table between the two of you. Instead of setting your differences on it, set down, one at a time, the things you both care about: the people you love, honesty, a good day's work, maybe a God you each pray to in your own way. Look at what's on the table. Find one sentence you could both say and mean. Hold it. The bell holds the time.
Kalimatin sawa'. A word level between us, the invitation of 3:64 to the People of the Scripture. Today's word.
Your line: start from what is shared. Today, in one conversation that could turn into an argument, start by saying out loud the thing you both agree on. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims cite 3:64 in interfaith conversation; in 2007 Muslim scholars and leaders addressed an open letter titled 'A Common Word Between Us and You' to Christian leaders, built on love of God and love of neighbor.

fork.setup: you invite someone to a word common between you. they turn away. what does 3:64 say to do?
options: say: bear witness that we are those who have surrendered to God.
fork.reveal: the verse simply asks them to witness where Muslims stand. no threat, no pursuit.

original.note: Arabic: a word level, equal, between us (3:64).

trapdoor: what you thought: a common word means a word everyone uses.
what it means: a word level between two sides, an invitation to the ground the verse sees as shared.
what a scholar hears: sawa', equal, even; a verse tied in tafsir to the Najran delegation, in hadith to the letter to Heraclius, and in 2007 to an open letter on love of God and neighbor.
